chunks: "I'd build it up in stages. The simplest driver, one direction, is an N-channel MOSFET as a low-side switch.
The motor goes between the supply and the drain, the source goes to ground, and the MCU's PWM pin drives the gate through about 100 ohms with a pull-down resistor so the motor is off during reset.
The crucial part is a flyback diode across the motor, a Schottky or fast diode with the cathode at the supply.
When the MOSFET turns off, the winding's current has to go somewhere, and without the diode the inductive kick would produce a voltage spike far above the supply and kill the transistor.
I'd also add a bulk capacitor at the supply to handle the PWM current pulses. For direction I'd use an H-bridge: four switches, with the motor in the middle.
Turning on the diagonal pair gives one direction, the other diagonal reverses it.
The big rule is never turn on both switches in the same leg, which is shoot-through, so the driver inserts dead time. In practice I'd use an integrated H-bridge or a gate driver.
For speed, PWM the drive: average voltage is duty times supply, and the motor's inductance smooths the current. About 20 kilohertz keeps it inaudible.
For accurate speed I'd close the loop with an encoder.

If isolation is required, between a mains-side or high-voltage motor and the MCU, I'd put an optocoupler or a digital isolator on the control lines, with an isolated gate driver and an isolated supply on the power side, so no ground connection exists between the two domains."
